title: Families flock to Delmarva Pride Festival
author: BROOKE ENSMINGER
content:
Families flock to Delmarva Pride Festival

 June 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BROOKE ENSMINGER | Section: News 
 
 582
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The fourth annual Delmarva Pride Festival brought together both young and old last weekend. Notable among the festivalgoers were families with young children.In recent years, the Pride Festival has faced defunding threats from several Easton Town Council members, who have argued that certain aspects of the event could be harmful to children. However, the festival organizers have made an effort to make the event family-friendly and appropriate for young children.
Kyle O'Donnell, the treasurer and co-founder of the Delmarva Pride Center, said the Center strives to create a welcoming environment for everyone.
"We thought that by default, Pride on the Shore should be family-friendly," O'Donnell said. "And to us, that meant asking the musical performers and bands to review their songs and we ask them to please not sing any songs or do any dance routines with curse words in them."
Many parents take their children each year, saying the event provides an opportunity to instill inclusivity from an early age.
Erin Shimko, of Easton, attended the festival with her husband and two children. She said she brings her children to help normalize self-expression and authenticity.
"We live nearby, so we've been going to this ever since we moved here," Schimko said. "So, it's just part of their life, and they don't question it."
Some attendees, like April Schmidt, drove an hour from Annapolis to attend the Pride Festival in Easton, where her children's grandparents live nearby in Preston. She was joined by her wife, their two children and the children's grandparents. Schmidt has a 2-year-old son and a 5-month-old daughter.
"I think it's really special for them to see other families that are similar to ours, but also just to celebrate Pride month in general, so they get a feel for accepting all," Schmidt said.
Many parents said they appreciated the positivity at the festival, with attendees smiling and enjoying themselves. Local Easton resident Angie Lavezzo walked around the festival with her two children and said she enjoyed the welcoming atmosphere.
"You're getting hugs from strangers, and everybody's so kind to each other," Lavezzo said. "It's just such a powerful statement of love."
Similar to many parents at the festival, Lavezzo brought her children to the event to show them people being "who they are to their core" and to teach them to accept everyone.
Some parents expressed gratitude for having a Pride Festival and a space to promote inclusivity in such a small town.
Blakely Barlev attended the festival for the first time with her daughter. A former New York resident, Barlev now lives in Easton and said it is important for children growing up in small towns to go to events like these since they aren't as frequently exposed to other communities.
"I lived in New York City for a while, so I'm used to seeing that all the time, but they don't," Barlev said. "So, I love bringing them to places like this, and I think it inspires them to be quirky and weird and be themselves."
Some parents offered suggestions on how the festival could become more engaging for children. Jaclyne Schettini, of Cambridge, said she remembered the festival having face painting in the past and would like to see it again. This year's festival had a temporary tattoo station instead.
Schmidt said she had been to other festivals with designated kids' areas and thinks that could be a good addition to the Delmarva Pride Festival going forward. But each parent interviewed said they would return for next year's festival to continue showing their children the importance of inclusivity.

title: DEI is about giving everybody an opportunity
author: STEPHEN RIDEOUT
content:
DEI is about giving everybody an opportunity

 June 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STEPHEN RIDEOUT | Section: Columns 
 
 600
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I am reading "How We Learn to Be Brave" by Bishop Mariann Edgar Budde, the Episcopal bishop of Washington.In her book, she writes about Thurgood Marshall and the challenges that he faced during his life.
"When he was denied admission to the University of Maryland School of Law on the basis of race, he reluctantly applied to Howard University School of Law, which he considered a far less reputable institution," she writes.
That interested me because I was aware that when he became a lawyer, he and the NAACP successfully sued the University of Maryland Law School in the case of Murray v. Pearson for denying Black students admission because of their race. It also interested me because of conversations I had with two men who had similar experiences.
One was a retired judge, who told me that he had gone to Howard and graduated as valedictorian. Thurgood Marshall asked him to apply to the University of Virginia Law School thinking that they would deny him admission, despite his qualifications, so that he could be Marshall's plaintiff in a lawsuit against the university.
When he applied to UVA, he was not denied admission. Rather, he was approached by a wealthy benefactor of the university with the offer to pay for his law education at any other law school that would accept him. The retired judge accepted the offer, went to law school in New York, and had to tell Mr. Marshall that he would not be the plaintiff in that lawsuit.
Gregory Swanson became the successful plaintiff in that lawsuit against the rector and Visitors of the University of Virginia brought by the NAACP with Thurgood Marshall being one of the lawyers where Mr. Swanson was granted admission to the law school.
Several years after my discussion with the retired judge, I had a chance meeting with Rep. Alcee Hastings from Florida. I sat near him on a plane trip and told him the story of the experience the retired judge had as a student. Interestingly, Congressman Hastings told me that it was not an isolated event, as the same thing had happened to him and had also happened to African Americans who had applied to medical schools in the South.
Schools and alumni offered to pay their way to a graduate school in the north to avoid the litigation that might come from the denial of admission to the school to which they applied. While some may have been denied admittance, others were offered some benefit to go elsewhere such as the payment of their tuition at a law school or medical school elsewhere in the U.S.
When I hear complaints about diversity, equity and inclusion, I never hear the full story of the background or reasoning for these complaints. I see the DEI effort not as promoting unqualified people to a position but rather giving all people the opportunity to be considered for a position who might otherwise be excluded from being considered. Giving everyone the opportunity to compete and learn from the experience, whether hired, admitted or not, seems to me to benefit everyone.
Colleges and universities have done something similar for many years for the children of alumni of their institutions where the child might not be considered the most qualified candidate but is admitted. How is that not favoritism based on connections rather than on skills and past accomplishments? In Cambridge during my time in city government, the search for qualified city employees included anyone interested and always tried to find people who were a good fit for our community who had the potential to become great and long-term workers for the city.

title: Kent chapter of Delmarva Pride hosts 'Authentic Selves' exhibit at Garfield Center
author: Staff Writer
content:
Kent chapter of Delmarva Pride hosts 'Authentic Selves' exhibit at Garfield Center

 June 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Local News 
 
 297
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — The Kent County chapter of the Delmarva Pride Center is proud to announce that it will host the powerful photo exhibit "Authentic Selves: Celebrating Trans and Nonbinary People and Their Families" at the Garfield Center for the Arts in Chestertown throughout the month of June, in honor of Pride Month.Developed by Family Diversity Projects, "Authentic Selves" is a traveling exhibit that uses photography and personal narratives to amplify the voices and lived experiences of transgender and nonbinary people across the United States. Each portrait is paired with heartfelt stories that explore the joys, challenges and resilience of individuals and their families.
Photographs by Robin Rayne, Gigi Kaeser, Jill Meyers and others. Interviews by Peggy Gillespie.
"The Authentic Selves exhibit offers an intimate and deeply moving look at trans and nonbinary lives," said Francoise Sullivan, chair of the Kent County chapter. "At a time when LGBTQIA+ communities, particularly trans individuals, are facing increasing scrutiny and threats across the country, this exhibit offers both visibility and celebration."
The exhibit will be on display in the lobby at the Garfield Center for the Arts, located at 210 High St., Chestertown, through June 30. Visitors can view the exhibit in the lobby during Tuesday Pride Center drop-in hours, 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. or regular Garfield Center box office hours Wednesday-Friday, 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. To schedule a visit outside of normal hours, please contact Francoise Sullivan at info@dpckentcounty.org.
The Kent County chapter of the Delmarva Pride Center invites residents and visitors to engage with "Authentic Selves" as part of a broader celebration of Pride Month, which includes a variety of events aimed at fostering inclusion, education, and support for LGBTQIA+ individuals and their families. For more information about the exhibit and other chapter events in Kent County, please visit www.dpckentcounty.org.

title: Native American communities underscore untold stories of American independence
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Native American communities underscore untold stories of American independence

 July 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 656
 Words 

 Read News Document

 VIENNA — July 4 is a day many Americans celebrate to honor the country's independence from Great Britain. For many Native Americans, the meaning behind the holiday is more complicated, and their story of Independence Day often goes overlooked.The narrative surrounding Fourth of July often highlights the triumphs of American independence while overlooking the injustices that accompanied it.
Native Americans existed on this continent long before white colonial settlers, and according to Director of Native American Studies at the University of South Carolina Lancaster, Stephen Criswell, The American Revolution likely would not have been accomplished without the help of the Indigenous population.
"It is less likely there would have been a successful revolution, we may have ended up as Canada or Australia," Criswell said on indigenous participation in the Revolutionary War. "That doesn't really get acknowledged," he said.
Donna "Wolf Mother" Abbott, chief of the Nause-Waiwash Band of Indians based in Dorchester County, said the story of July 4 is bigger than the colonists gaining independence from Great Britain.
She said it is important to tell the whole story.
"When the colonists came here, the Native Americans were already free, and the colonists had to experience our lifestyle, our culture and our traditions," Abbott said. "What they experienced and what they learned from us was a part of the story that's missing."
Criswell said while the Declaration of Independence called Native Americans "merciless Indian Savages," those who wrote it relied heavily on the indigenous peoples' knowledge of the land.
"You know, they called them savages but shortly after referred to them as the Five Civilized Tribes, so which is it?" Criswell asked. "Of course, this is the same document that says all men are created equal, except for those that don't own land, or aren't white or aren't male," Criswell said.
The wording of the Declaration of Independence underscored a pervasive attitude that dictated centuries of discriminatory policies toward Native American people, including forced displacement, land theft and suppression of identity.
Criswell said July 4 is a holiday that's not as hotly debated among Native American communities as other holidays, like Christopher Colombus Day. Usually, he said, the Fourth of July is an opportunity for family and friends to come together.
The Fourth of July has historically been an opportunity for Native American people to practice their own ceremonies, especially in the late 1800s, when Congress passed the Religious Crimes Code, banning all Native American ceremonies and dancing, according to Smithsonian Magazine.
For 50 years, Native Americans either held religious ceremonies in secret or didn't have them at all due to the extremely harsh punishments like imprisonment or withholding treaty rations. Indigenous ceremonies during this time were held on or near July 4 under the guise of American celebration. Because of this, many tribal gatherings today take place on or near the Fourth of July, according to the Indigenous Foundation.
While there is no formal Nause‑Waiwash event on July 4, Abbott said members of the tribe do celebrate the holiday. "It's a celebration where families get together and spend time together, and we are all about family and friendship," Abbott said about the holiday.
Abbott said a good way to honor Native Americans on the Fourth of July is to tell the whole story of American independence and to learn more about Indigenous history. "I find a good resource is the Maryland Archives," she said.
In 2023, The state of Maryland began the Indigenous Archive Project for the Eastern Shore of Maryland where seven members from different tribal communities record and keep their oral histories. This archive is publicly accessible.
Within the Maryland Archives, stories of Indigenous veterans of the Revolutionary War can be found.
The Nause-Waiwash Band of Indians will hold its 33rd annual festival on Sept. 13 of this year. "Each year we have tried to do something a little different and add something to it that's different so we don't fall into the rut of having the same thing every year, so we're proud of that," Abbott said.

title: Cambridge becomes a Just Community
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Cambridge becomes a Just Community

 July 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 634
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — On Juneteenth at Bethel AME Church on Pine Street, Gov. Wes Moore announced the Just Communities designation of 419 locations across Maryland, including parts of Cambridge. Moore said it was not a coincidence this announcement was made in a city where the Civil Rights Movement took center stage.The Moore-Miller administration established the Just Communities Designation in 2024 to address policies that have disenfranchised generations of families, such as redlining and exclusionary zoning.
"We wanted to hold it in one of the communities that rose to the top tier of places that had experienced the most harm and from which, the least improvement has occurred," said Secretary of Housing and Community Development Jake Day of the Juneteenth event.
The initiative is the result of work by The Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development Division of Just Communities. Day said he has worked closely with Division of Just Communities Assistant Secretary Cat Goughnour.
Day said the Just Communities Act not only acknowledges past harms but returns resources to those communities. As part of the initiative, Day said Cambridge residents will see community-nominated projects for revitalization, such as facilities, housing and economic developments.
"We want to make sure that we understand what the community wants and not show up with development when people aren't asking for it," he said.
According to Day, early indicators of success for the Just Communities Act would be more project activity in neighborhoods with visible scars, like the Pine Street corridor of Cambridge, formerly known as Black Wall Street.
This could include more home repairs for legacy homeowners, increased homeownership, new homes on vacant lots, new community buildings and more businesses. Long term outcomes include improved public health and reduced criminal justice involvement, Day said.
Cambridge Mayor Lajan Cephas said she feels this is a framework for justice. With Cambridge's history of slavery, Jim Crow, discriminatory policies and segregation among wards, Cephas is hopeful the Just Communities designation will begin to rectify past harms.
"It's being unwound," Cephas said. "It's just great to finally address, you know, the financial instabilities and other opportunities that were held back in communities just like Cambridge."
Cephas said along with the investments made in the community, the Just Communities initiative pushes grant requests to the front of the line.
"I say, Gov. Moore, it's like you gave us platform shoes," she said. "It's very difficult competing against these other municipalities. They have better grant writers, better budgets. You know, they have comprehensive plans that they've been working on for years, and we're just now getting caught up."
Cephas wants to make it clear that these initiatives will not solely benefit Black residents, but will benefit all residents who have been affected by discriminatory policies and live within the Just Communities designated area, which encompasses much of downtown Cambridge and surrounding neighborhoods.
The Just Communities Act has faced pushback from Maryland Republican lawmakers, who called the initiative an unproductive government handout and unfair to Maryland taxpayers, according to a statement issued to the Baltimore Sun.
In a statement to the Star Democrat Friday morning, Maryland Senate Minority Leader Stephen Hershey (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) said, "Does anyone really believe pumping hundreds of millions into handpicked areas will build generational wealth?"
"This is wealth redistribution dressed up in equity language — it's socialism, plain and simple," the statement said.
But the initiative's proponents contend the Just Communities designations aim to ensure fairness among Maryland residents.
"It's the very picture of fairness as I was raised and taught to understand fairness," Day said. "Again, take something from somebody and you return it."
Cephas echoed Day's sentiments, pointing to the "unfair" practices that have held Cambridge back.
The community can check on updates for the Just Communities Designation at choosecambridge.com, where residents can sign up for public alerts via text or email.
This report has been updated to include comments from Sen. Stephen Hershey.
